Vallouise
val-weez'
n. (Dauphine valley above Briancçon, renamed for Louis the Eleventh; a Waldensian valley attacked in 1488)
French Vallouise, the valley of Louis, renamed in honour of Louis the Eleventh; its earlier name was the Vallis Puta, which the older spelling rendered unflatteringly.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Vallouise is the valley of the Gyronde above Briancon in the Dauphine, and before its renaming in the fifteenth century it was one of the Waldensian valleys of the French Alps. In the campaign of 1488, part of the crusade published the previous year by Innocent the Eighth, the troops under the legate's authority came up the valley and the inhabitants withdrew to the high ground and into the caves above it, as they had done before. This time the troops followed. The account, which comes in substance from the proceedings themselves as well as from the later Protestant historians, is that fires were lit at the mouths of the caves and that those inside, said to have been many score and chiefly women, children and the old, died there. Such of the people as survived conformed or came down from the valley, and Vallouise, unlike Freissinieres, ceased to be a Waldensian place. The dictionary enters it as the plainest answer to a question the valleys raise, which is why the Alpine Waldensians survived in Piedmont and not in Dauphine. They survived where the ground was defensible and the prince was weak, and they were destroyed where it was not, and the difference was not their faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cave as a hollow place in the earth; smothering as the suffocating by excluding air; and extinction as the putting an end to, a destroying utterly.

expand to see more

CAVE, n. [L. cavus, hollow.] A hollow place in the earth; a subterraneous cavern; a den.

SMOTHER, v.t. To suffocate or extinguish life by causing smoke or dust to be inhaled, or by excluding air.

EXTINCTION, n. [L. extinctio.] The act of putting out or destroying light or fire; destruction; suppression; a putting an end to.

CONFORM, v.i. To comply with or yield to; to live or act according to, as a rule or an established church.

DEFENSIBLE, adj. That may be defended; capable of being maintained or justified.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:38 — "(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth."

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Psa 34:19 — "Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all."

Lam 3:22 — "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."

Modern Corruption

Dauphine valley whose Waldensian people were destroyed in the caves above it in 1488, and which ceased after that to be a Waldensian place.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the completed persecution—the case in which the persecutor wins. The dictionary records it deliberately, because the histories of the valleys are written from the places that survived, and a reader who sees only Angrogna and Torre Pellice may conclude that faithfulness and survival go together. They do not. Vallouise was as faithful as the Val Pellice and it was wiped out, and the difference lay in the gradient of the ground and the strength of the local prince.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence is not a reward scheme. “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38) is said in a chapter which has just distinguished those who escaped the edge of the sword from those who were slain by it, and commends both. “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed” (Lam 3:22) is the right word in the mouth of a survivor, and it is not an explanation of why the others were.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek spelaion (G4693), a cave or den; Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy.

expand to see more

Greek spelaion (G4693) — a cave, a den; “in dens and caves of the earth”, Hebrews 11:38.

Greek planao (G4105) — to wander, to be driven about; “they wandered in deserts”, Hebrews 11:38.

Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay; “the souls of them that were slain”, Revelation 6:9.

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to snatch away, to deliver; “the LORD delivereth him out of them all”, Psalm 34:19.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, covenant kindness; “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed”, Lamentations 3:22.

Usage

"“they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38) — the caves above the valley, 1488."

"“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — a persecution that succeeded, and is therefore seldom told."

"“It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed” (Lam 3:22) — the right word for a survivor, and not an explanation."
